title: Design a Rate Limiter
tagline: Cap how many requests a client can make — the algorithm, where it lives, and how to make it work across a fleet.
summary: Token bucket in Redis, where to place it, distributed counting.

blocks.title: Functional
items: Limit each client to N requests per time window (e.g., 100 req/min per user/API key/IP).
Reject excess requests with HTTP 429 + a Retry-After header.
Support different limits for different routes/tiers (free vs paid).

blocks.title: Non-functional
items: Low latency — it sits on every request, so it must add minimal overhead.
Accurate enough — strictly correct limits are nice but a tiny over/under-count is usually acceptable.
Highly available & distributed — must work consistently across many server instances.
Fail open vs fail closed — decide what happens if the limiter's store is down.

paragraphs: Rate limiting is a cross-cutting concern, so it usually lives at the edge — in the **API gateway / reverse proxy** — so abusive traffic is rejected *before* it reaches and wastes backend capacity. It can also be a dedicated middleware or a sidecar. Putting it client-side alone is insufficient (clients can't be trusted), and putting it deep in each service duplicates logic.

Key design choice: the counters must be **shared** across all gateway/server instances, or a client spread across instances bypasses the limit. So the limiter's state lives in a fast central store — almost always **Redis**.

blocks.caption: The limiter at the edge checks a shared Redis counter; over-limit requests get 429 before touching backends.

paragraphs: Default to **token bucket**: each key (user/API key) has a bucket holding up to `capacity` tokens, refilled at `rate` tokens/sec. Each request removes one token; if the bucket is empty, reject with 429. This caps the average rate while allowing short bursts up to the bucket size — matching real client behaviour and cheap to compute. (Alternatives: leaky bucket smooths to a fixed rate; sliding-window counter is most accurate but heavier; fixed-window is simplest but allows a 2x boundary burst.)

codes.title: model

blocks.title: It must be atomic
blocks.text: Read-modify-write on the counter must be atomic, or concurrent requests race and over-admit. In Redis, do it in a single atomic operation — a Lua script (read tokens, refill, decrement, write) or atomic INCR with expiry for window counters. Never read then write in two separate round trips.

items.detail: All instances update the same per-key bucket atomically, so the limit is global regardless of which instance handles the request.
A Redis round trip per request adds latency. Mitigate by colocating Redis, pipelining, or giving each instance a small local token lease it syncs periodically (trading a little precision for speed).

If Redis is unavailable: fail-open (allow requests) keeps the product up but drops protection; fail-closed (reject) protects backends but causes an outage. Most pick fail-open for user-facing traffic, fail-closed for protecting fragile/expensive backends. State the choice explicitly.
Limit per API key (paying customers), per user id (logged-in), or per IP (anonymous) — or layered. IP alone is weak (NAT, shared IPs, spoofing).

blocks.text: One-sentence answer to 'design a rate limiter': 'Token bucket per key stored in Redis, updated atomically with a Lua script, enforced at the API gateway; return 429 + Retry-After; fail-open if Redis is down; optimize with local token leases.' Then expand on whichever part they probe.

cheatsheet: Place the limiter at the edge (API gateway) to reject abuse before it hits backends; client-side alone can't be trusted.
Default algorithm: token bucket (caps average rate, allows bursts); know leaky/fixed/sliding-window alternatives.
Counters must be SHARED across instances (Redis) and updated ATOMICALLY (Lua script) or requests race/over-admit.
Return 429 + Retry-After; key by API key/user/IP (IP alone is weak).
Decide fail-open (availability) vs fail-closed (protection) if the store is down; optimize latency with local token leases.

questions.prompt: Two requests from the same user arrive at two different gateway instances at the exact same moment when only one token remains. Both check Redis, see 1 token, and both allow. What's the bug and the fix?
answer: It's a race condition from a non-atomic read-modify-write: both instances read `tokens = 1`, both decide there's a token available, both decrement and allow — admitting 2 requests when only 1 was permitted. Under load this lets clients consistently exceed the limit.

Fix it by making the check-and-decrement **atomic** at the store. In Redis, run a single Lua script that reads the bucket, refills, decrements if a token is available, and writes back — executed atomically so the second request sees the first's decrement and is correctly rejected. (Equivalent atomic primitives: `INCR`+expiry for window counters, or `SET`/`EVAL` transactions.) The principle: never split the counter update across two round trips.
keyPoints: Make check+decrement atomic (single Redis Lua script)
Second request observes the decrement and is rejected
followUps: How would per-instance local token leases change the accuracy guarantee?

questions.prompt: Your Redis (the limiter's store) goes down. Should the rate limiter fail open or fail closed? How do you decide?
questions.hint: What's worse: an outage, or temporarily unprotected backends?
answer: It depends on what you're protecting. **Fail-open** (allow requests when Redis is unavailable) keeps the product working for users but temporarily removes rate-limit protection — risky if the backend is fragile or the limit guards against cost/abuse. **Fail-closed** (reject when you can't verify the limit) protects the backend but turns a Redis blip into a full user-facing outage.

For most user-facing traffic, fail-open is the common choice — availability of the product usually outweighs brief loss of throttling, and a Redis outage is rare and short. For limiters protecting expensive or easily-overwhelmed downstreams (e.g., a costly third-party API or a fragile legacy system), fail-closed (or a conservative local fallback limit) is safer. The key is to make this a *deliberate, stated* decision and to also build Redis HA (replication/cluster) so the question rarely arises.
keyPoints: Fail-open = availability but no protection; fail-closed = protection but outage
User-facing traffic usually fail-open; fragile/costly backends fail-closed
Or fall back to a conservative local limit
Make Redis HA so the failure is rare; state the choice explicitly
followUps: How could a local in-memory fallback limit work during a Redis outage?
